Article Title: Asian Games Medal Tally: India win 8 medals but remain outside top 10 as gold continues to elude
Article Text:
Yashvir Singh, Rohit Yadav, and Esha Singh

Eight medals, but no gold for India

Shooting and kurash add to India's tally

NEW DELHI: India produced another strong medal haul at the Asian Games 2026 on Monday, winning eight medals across athletics, shooting and kurash. However, the impressive collection did not bring any change in the overall standings, with India remaining 12th as the country continued to wait for another gold medal.India added four silver and four bronze medals during the day but could not increase its gold tally. After Day 9, India stood at 45 medals — four gold, 20 silver and 21 bronze.'The eight-medal haul included silver medals for Yashvir Singh, Murali Sreeshankar, Gulveer Singh and Esha Singh, while Rohit Yadav, Parul Chaudhary, Vithya Ramraj and Pincky Balhara won bronze.India's strongest showing came in the men's javelin, where Yashvir and Rohit produced a double podium finish in the absence of defending champion Neeraj Chopra.Yashvir recorded a personal best of 85.72m for silver, while Rohit won bronze with 84.35m. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage claimed gold with 88.55m.Sreeshankar also won silver in the men's long jump with 8.07m despite an injury forcing him to abandon his final two attempts. China's Yuhao Shi took gold with 8.17m.Gulveer added his second silver of the Games with a personal best of 3:36.72 in the men's 1500m, having earlier finished runner-up in the 10,000m.Parul Chaudhary won bronze in the women's 5000m with 15:14.61, adding to the bronze she had claimed in the 3000m steeplechase.Vithya Ramraj also took bronze in the women's 400m hurdles with a personal best of 54.75 seconds.Esha Singh secured silver in the women's 25m pistol after finishing with 38 hits, the same score as China's Xiao Jiaruixuan, who won the gold after the shoot-off.Pincky Balhara added bronze in the women's -78kg kurash category, losing 0-5 to South Korea's Sumin Mo in the semifinals.Despite the eight medals, India's gold tally remained at four, a crucial factor in the standings as countries are ranked by gold medals first.China led with 132 golds, followed by Japan with 41, South Korea with 21 and Uzbekistan with 12. India remained 12th with 45 medals, highlighting how a large haul of silver and bronze medals has yet to translate into a significant rise in the standings.
Article Summary: India added four silver and four bronze medals during the day but could not increase its gold tally. China led with 132 golds, followed by japan with 41, south korea with 21 and uzbekistan with 12. India remained 12th with 45 medals, highlighting how a large haul of silver and bronze medals has yet to translate into a significant rise in the standings.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to hear next week a petition filed against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, seeking his suspension and a declaration that the CEC cannot take unilateral decisions on the Election Commission ’s behalf.The petition also sought that special intensive revision of electoral rolls and all actions, decisions, directions and consequential measures undertaken pursuant to the exercise be declared void ab initio (invalid) and without lawful authority.The plea was mentioned by senior advocate Vikas Singh before CJI Surya Kant.Petitioner Rakesh Kumar Singh alleged that about 14 decisions were taken in the EC’s name despite objections recorded by the two other election commissioners, S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.He sought a direction to the CEC to “show under what authority he has acted, and continues to act” as though he is individually entitled to exercise the collective decision-making power vested by Article 324 of the Constitution in the EC.Significantly, CEC has asserted that all decisions regarding SIR were taken unanimously by all election commissioners.

Article Title: Brij Bhushan acquittal challenged over ‘stereotypical assumptions’ about sexual assault victims
Article Text:
Wrestlers challenge acquittal, cite ‘stereotypical assumptions’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Rouse Avenue court has issued notice to former Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh and others on an appeal challenging his acquittal in a sexual harassment case involving women wrestlers.Special Judge Dig Vinay Singh sought a response to the appeal and listed the matter for hearing on October 9. The court also directed that the original affidavit and orders containing the names of the victims be placed in a sealed envelope. It further directed the appellant to file a copy of the petition with the victims’ names redacted.The appeal challenges the August 3 order of the Rouse Avenue court, Brij Bhushan and Vinod Tomar in the case. The wrestlers have contended that the acquittal order is unsustainable in law and is based on a “manifestly erroneous and selective appreciation of the evidence on record”.The appeal has contended that the impugned order proceeds on conjectures and surmises, fails to apply binding and well-settled principles of law, and, in material part, rests its reasoning on “archaic and stereotypical assumptions” about the “expected” behaviour of victims of sexual assault and harassment, rather than on a fair, evidence-based assessment after taking into account the circumstances of the victims.The case stems from an FIR filed by Delhi Police following a complaint by a woman wrestler during Singh’s tenure as WFI chief. The police had invoked Sections 354, 354-D, 354-A, 506(1) and 109 of the Indian Penal Code.Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Ashwani Panwar had acquitted Singh and Tomar after a trial that was conducted in a closed courtroom. The two were tried in connection with allegations of sexual harassment of women wrestlers in India and abroad.Delhi Police had filed a 1,500-page charge sheet against Singh and Tomar on June 15, 2023, following its investigation into the allegations.The women wrestlers had earlier staged a protest at Jantar Mantar, following which the FIR was registered by Delhi Police based on the complaint.Advocate Rajiv Mohan, assisted by Rehan Khan and Rishabh Bhati, represented Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh, while senior advocate Rebecca John appeared for the victims and complainants.
Article Summary: Wrestlers challenge acquittal, cite ‘stereotypical assumptions’ special judge dig vinay singh sought a response to the appeal and listed the matter for hearing on october 9. The appeal challenges the august 3 order of the rouse avenue court, brij bhushan and vinod tomar in the case.

Article Title: 'Look into her eyes': Neeru Dhanda's hospital scare, 2 Asian Games golds and the 'fire' Mansher Singh saw
Article Text:
Neeru Dhanda (Image credit: PTI)

‘Winning the World Cup and Asian Games in the same year is incredible’

Neeru Dhanda and Mansher Singh (Image credit: Special arrangement)

‘The Olympic medal is the first thing’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Neeru Dhanda does not need to be aggressive to show her competitive side. “Look into her eyes,” says Mansher Singh, her coach of seven years.The 25-year-old shooter on Tuesday became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games gold in trap, following her World Cup triumph in Italy in July. For Mansher, who has watched Neeru develop since she was 18, the performance was another expression of a quality he has seen throughout her career.“She has a lot of fire in her belly. If in the final, she will go all guns blazing and that’s what she did,” Mansher told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.Neeru shot 28 in the final in Aichi-Nagoya, surpassing the previous Asian record of 24. She had earlier won a silver medal in the women's trap team event at the Games.The Asian Games gold came less than three months after Neeru became the first Indian woman to win an individual World Cup gold in trap, at the Shotgun World Cup in Italy. At Aichi-Nagoya, after the individual gold, she claimed her second gold in the mixed team events to add to the silver she clicnhed in the women’s team trap event.“She is not aggressive at all. If you want to see the aggression, look into her eyes,” Mansher said.“I’m just proud and happy that she’s got what she deserves because she’s very hardworking and very determined to be successful and, more importantly, to achieve. She has achieved things which have not happened in the past.”Mansher believes the back-to-back titles have changed the conversation around his student.“So she wants to go to new heights, and this is exactly what she’s doing now. She’s won the last two big competitions. She’ll be the first Indian woman to do this, you know. So, winning the World Cup and Asian Games in the same year, almost back to back, is incredible,” he said.Neeru's rise has also been accompanied by a change in the way she handles the pressure around her.“She used to fight with me a lot. Then I would say, ‘I’m like your father.’ Then she would say, ‘Yes, I can’t fight with my father.’ Then she would come back to normal,” Mansher recalled.“But she was an emotional person. She’s much more mature now. She’s able to take her decisions and think about the consequences.”The coach was also closely involved when Neeru fell ill shortly before the Asian Games.She was admitted to PSRI Hospital in Chirag Delhi after a viral fever did not improve with medication. Even while on the hospital bed, Mansher said, Neeru remained focused on the competition ahead.“Sir, medal lana hai desh ke liye. This is all she had been saying while on the hospital bed. I was just happy and worried at the same time,” he recalled.Neeru was discharged and travelled to Japan without much time to recover.Mansher's message to her before she left was simple.“You should be happy that God has blessed you with the opportunity to go after being so sick for eight days that you were in hospital. Enjoy yourself and celebrate,” he told her.With the World Cup and Asian Games titles now secured in the same year, attention will turn to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.India's last Olympic shotgun medal came through Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore, who won silver in men's double trap at Athens 2004. Since then, India have not won an Olympic medal in shotgun.Mansher, who represented India at four Olympics - Los Angeles 1984, Atlanta 1996, Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008 - said the Olympic target has long been part of their conversations.“I think we don’t have to worry about that. She’s very centred. She knows that’s her goal. She’s not going to take a gold medal at the World Cup and at the Asian Games and make it so big that she loses sight of her ultimate goal,” Mansher said.“And it’s always been a conversation amongst us that, you know, the Olympic medal is the first thing. The Olympics are the first and last thing in this sport.”For Mansher, the two gold medals have provided something more useful than simply another set of titles.“But overall, there’s proof enough to say that you are definitely in that league or in that conversation to be a medalist at the Olympics,” he said.
Article Summary: Neeru dhanda became the first indian woman to win an individual asian games gold in trap. The 25-year-old shot 28 in the final in aichi-nagoya, surpassing the previous asian record of 24. She had earlier won a silver medal in the women's trap team event at the games.

Article Title: 'Major posting' for Shoaib Akhtar? Mohsin Naqvi holds talks with former Pakistan star
Article Text:

PCB plans wider overhaul

From critic to decision-maker?

Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar could soon move from being one of the Pakistan Cricket Board’s most vocal critics to having a role in shaping its cricketing decisions.Akhtar is reportedly in line for a major position within the PCB as chairman Mohsin Naqvi looks to restructure the board’s cricket think tank following Pakistan’s disastrous tour of England, PTI reported. While the exact nature of the proposed role has not been formally announced, Akhtar and Naqvi have already held discussions over Pakistan cricket.A source close to the PCB said Akhtar, who resides in Islamabad, met Naqvi last week and the two spoke at length about cricket-related matters.“Few weeks back when Shoaib’s elder brother passed away Mohsin Naqvi had interacted with him closely and was there for him. This gesture impressed Shoaib a lot who has been a vocal critic of the PCB and Pakistan cricket in the past in his media appearances,” the source added.The relationship between the two has since strengthened, with Naqvi also sharing his plans with Akhtar and inviting him to visit the National Cricket Academy (NCA) and training camps.“Shoaib is in line to get a major posting but obviously when he met with the Chairman he had his own set of ideas and conditions through which he believes Pakistan cricket can be taken forward,” the source said.Akhtar's potential appointment comes as the PCB considers changes beyond the senior men's team.The board is also exploring the possibility of bringing in foreign coaches and consultants following the departures of senior team fielding coach Shane McDermott and batting coach Ashley Noffke.The women's national team is another area under review, with the PCB considering the appointment of a permanent long-term head coach.“The board is working on some plans for the future and there will be some changes in the cricket think tank soon because the Chairman has made it clear that he expects better results from the national mens, womens, shaheens and junior teams,” the source stated.The proposed restructuring follows a difficult period for Pakistan cricket, particularly after the men's team's Test series in England.Pakistan were beaten 3-0 in the series, suffering a first-ever clean sweep in a Test series on English soil. The result has increased scrutiny on the national side as well as the wider cricketing structure surrounding it. In the middle of the series, Pakistan sent back seven players, including Mohammed Rizwan and Imam-ul-Haq, as well as head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul. Mike Hesson was subsequently asked to fill the head coach role in the third Test.The PCB is therefore examining changes to its cricketing setup, including coaching and consultancy appointments, rather than restricting its response to the senior men's team.Akhtar has spent years speaking publicly about Pakistan cricket, regularly questioning selection decisions, administrative choices and the direction of the national team. His outspoken views have often made him a prominent critic of the PCB.A formal role within the board would therefore mark a significant change for the former fast bowler. Instead of analysing Pakistan cricket from outside the system, Akhtar could potentially have a direct say in the decisions and plans he has frequently commented on.The precise position being considered for him, however, is yet to be formally announced.
Article Summary: Shoaib akhtar is reportedly in line for a major position within the pakistan cricket board. The former fast bowler has held discussions with chairman mohsin naqvi about cricket-related matters. The pcb is also considering changes to its cricketing setup beyond the senior men's team.

Article Title: Lovlina Borgohain enters 75kg final, to fight for Asian Games gold
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: India's star boxer Lovlina Borgohain defeated Kazakhstan's Natalya Bogdanova to enter the women's 75kg final at the Nishio Gymnasium in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Wednesday.Lovlina, who won a silver medal at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, now has a chance to change the colour of her medal at the continental event.The Indian boxer won the closely fought semifinal on points. Article Title: Joga Purty breaks own national record again, storms into Asian Games quarterfinals
Article Text:
Joga Purty (right) during her event in Nagoya on Tuesday and (pic right) with her coach Babulal Rawat

Kolkata:

Joga Purty continued her rapid rise in Indian sport climbing by storming into the women’s speed climbing quarterfinals at the Asian Games on Tuesday while rewriting the national record yet again.The 19-year-old from Jamshedpur clocked 7.28 seconds in the qualification round at Portmesse Nagoya Exhibition Hall to finish ninth among Asia’s best speed climbers and secure a place in the knockout stage. In the process, she improved on her own national record of 7.37 seconds, a mark that had earned her a place in India’s Asian Games squad.The performance came as little surprise to those who have watched the teenager’s journey from close quarters.“Even when she first came to us in 2019, I felt there was something special about her,” said Babulal Rawat, her coach at the Tata Steel Adventure Foundation (TSAF) Climbing Academy. “Around 40 children had come for a trial, but the way she moved on the wall stood out immediately. She was climbing better than many athletes who had already been training for two or three years.”Purty’s road to the Asian Games has been far from smooth. Coming from a modest background in Jamshedpur, she was initially shy and often reluctant to compete.Today, however, she is among Asia’s top speed climbers.“There are very few female climbers in India who can match Joga’s level and pace during training. As a result, she often trains and races against boys,” said Rawat, a former climber who moved from Uttarakhand to Jamshedpur in 2014 and took up coaching in 2018. “That pushes her to compete harder every day and gives her an additional source of motivation.”The coach also stressed that international exposure would be critical if Purty has to fulfil her long-term potential.“When she goes abroad and trains against stronger climbers, that motivation becomes even greater, which is why international exposure is so important for her development,” he added.Purty’s 7.28-second effort, while a national record, also highlighted the gap that Indian climbers are trying to bridge at the highest level. China’s Lijuan Deng topped the qualification round with an Asian Games record of 6.23 seconds, while South Korea’s Jimin Jeong was second with a best time of 6.25 seconds.Rawat believes closing that gap will require sustained investment in the sport.“Sport climbing is still very new in India. Many people are not even aware of the sport. Athletes need regular international exposure and opportunities to compete against the world’s best. A short training trip abroad is not enough. If our climbers are to challenge for medals consistently, they need to compete internationally much more often,” he said.For now, though, his focus is on the knockout rounds of the Asian Games, where climbers race head-to-head on the 15-metre wall. Rawat believes Purty can lower the national record even further in Wednesday’s quarterfinal.“I still feel she can do even better. She has the talent to improve on her personal best,” he said.And judging by Tuesday’s performance, Purty has already shown she belongs among Asia’s elite, with the teenager from Jamshedpur continuing to push the boundaries of Indian sport climbing one national record at a time.
Article Summary: Joga purty clocked 7.28 seconds in the qualification round at portmesse nagoya exhibition hall to finish ninth among asia’s best speed climbers. In the process, she improved on her own national record of 7.37 seconds, a mark that had earned her a place in india's asian games squad.

Article Title: Priya Ghanghas clinches bronze at Asian Games after 1-4 defeat in 60kg semifinal
Article Text:

Indian boxer Priya Ghanghas signed off with a bronze medal after her Asian Games campaign ended with a 1-4 defeat to former world champion Yang Chengyu of China in the women's 60kg semifinal on Wednesday.The 20-year-old, making her Asian Games debut, found herself up against a considerably more experienced opponent but fought her way to a place on the podium with her run to the last four.Yang, a former world champion, prevailed in the semifinal to book her place in the gold-medal bout, while Priya settled for bronze.Priya's medal adds to India's strong showing in boxing at the Games. Indian boxers have already bettered their medal tally from the previous edition in Hangzhou, where they won one silver and three bronze medals, by ensuring a six-medal haul this time.Parveen Hooda in the women's 65kg category and Ankush Panghal in the men's 80kg event have already secured their places in the finals, with both gold-medal bouts scheduled for Friday.Super heavyweight boxer Narender Berwal also signed off with a bronze medal on Tuesday.India's boxing campaign is not over yet, with Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain and Kapil Pokhariya still in contention for a place in the gold-medal bout on Wednesday.Lovlina will compete in the women's 75kg category, while Kapil is in action in the men's 90kg event.India also added another gold medal on Wednesday as Chikitha Taniparthi and Sahil Jadhav won the compound mixed team title.The Indian pair edged Korea's Jungyoon Park and Choi Eun Gyu 158-157 after a tense shoot-off to claim gold and secure a 2028 Olympic quota place.Chikitha and Sahil had entered the final after beating Thailand 156-155 in the semifinals. China's Fangyao F Wei and Jinyi Liu won the bronze medal.Earlier, India's women's compound team retained its Asian Games title. Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Chikitha and Prithika Pradeep defeated China's Wunier, Yue Wang and Fangyao Wei 238-234 to finish on top with a world record-equalling score.Jyothi was also part of the Indian women's team that won gold at the Hangzhou Asian Games.
Article Summary: Priya ghanghas signs off with a bronze medal after losing to china's yang chengyu. Indian boxers have already bettered their medal tally from the previous edition in hangzhou. Chikitha taniparthi and sahil jadhav won the compound mixed team title.

Article Title: Gulveer Singh completes Asian Games medal treble after gruelling five-day athletics test
Article Text:
India's Gulveer Singh (AP/PTI)

Pooja jumps to bronze

Bronze in mixed relay

Nagoya: Before leaving for training or competitions, Gulveer Singh has a ritual he never skips. He prays to a small statue of Lord Hanuman that he carries with him everywhere and applies vermilion to his forehead.By the time he completed his 5000m race on Tuesday night, the red mark between his brows had long been washed away by rain and sweat. But the 29-year-old had left an indelible mark on the Asian Games, completing a treble of medals: a bronze in the 5000m to go with silvers in the 10,000m and 1500m.His week at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium has been defined by perseverance, discipline and versatility. Built on a staple diet of daal, roti, sabzi, paneer and protein supplements, his lean frame has carried him through three gruelling races in five days, producing a feat rarely seen in Indian athletics.Gulveer clocked a personal best of 13:32.75 to finish behind Bahrain’s Birhanu Balew (13:30.79) and Japan’s Tomonori Yamaguchi (13:31.43).The three-medal haul, he said, was the result of sticking religiously to his routines and his coach’s plans.“I set out with the target of wanting to win three medals and I’m happy to have achieved that. I just listen to what the coach tells me and follow his plans. I never say, ‘Today I won’t do this.’I follow the coach completely,” Gulveer said.Meanwhile, 3000m steeplechaser Avinash Sable , who finished fourth in his pet event, did not start.For a while, Pooja’s name at the top of the high-jump leaderboard offered the possibility of a golden leap. The 19-year-old, however, had to settle for bronze after clearing 1.84m.The national record holder was flawless through 1.70m, 1.75m, 1.80m and 1.84m, clearing each height on her first attempt. She then failed all three attempts at 1.87m, but her clean card at 1.84m was enough to earn her the final podium spot on countback.Harita Bhadra, a last-minute inclusion in the squad, justified her selection by anchoring India to bronze in the mixed 4x100m relay.The quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha Satyanarayana, Animesh Kujur and Harita timed a season-best 41.06 seconds.India were fourth heading into the final leg, but Harita, who won bronze in the 200m earlier in the Games, produced a strong finish to overtake Sri Lanka’s Shanthi Perera and bring India another bronze.China won gold in 40.78 seconds, while Thailand took silver in 40.87.India signed off their athletics campaign with one gold, nine silver and 14 bronze.
Article Summary: Gulveer singh won bronze in the 5000m to go with silvers in the 10,000m and 1500m. The 29-year-old clocked a personal best of 13:32.75 to finish behind bahrain's birhanu balew and japan's tomonori yamaguchi. Pooja jumped to bronze after clearing 1.84m.

Article Title: Chess Olympiad Round 9: D Gukesh channels his world champion self, overturns almost-lost game to keep India in gold hunt
Article Text:
Dommaraju Gukesh of India (Photo by Rafal Oleksiewicz for FIDE)

How Gukesh turned the tables on Donchenko

Vantika, Divya lead India's women to victory

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

ALSO READ:

NEW DELHI: Since becoming world champion two years ago, noise has followed Dommaraju Gukesh almost everywhere, at times making it feel as though he isn't worthy of the title he rightfully won.But on Friday, when India needed the youngest world champion in history to deliver a win, he did exactly that, turning around an almost-lost position to beat Germany's Alexander Donchenko in Round 9 of the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.It was the kind of performance that felt like it could quiet the criticism all on its own.Playing black, Gukesh traded off his dark-squared bishop early to damage White's pawn structure, then spent the middlegame manoeuvring patiently, repositioning knights, expanding on the queenside with a5-a4, and probing for weaknesses without rushing.For a long stretch, the position stayed murky and roughly balanced, with both sides shuffling pieces and neither able to land a clean blow.It was in the run-up to the time control that things turned dangerous for Gukesh. Donchenko doubled his rooks on the e-file and pushed one all the way to e6, aiming squarely at Black's king, which had been forced to step out to f7 for safety.With his own clock running low, Gukesh had to defend precisely while trying to generate counterplay of his own on the kingside, pushing his h- and g-pawns forward to create complications.It was a position where one careless move could have ended the game in White's favour.Gukesh held his nerve. As the pawn storms and piece trades settled down, he found a route to activate his queen and knight while White's pieces drifted out of coordination.The Chennai-born grandmaster found an excellent move with 51...Nf4. The German sacked Gukesh's knight with 52.Rxf4, but Donchenko's bishop was thus left hanging on c3; Gukesh's queen swooped in to capture it, and from there it was a matter of technique.A check with his queen forced Donchenko's king into an impossible spot, and White resigned rather than play on a piece down with his king exposed.Elsewhere on the board, Nihal Sarin, playing white, spent much of his game in some turmoil against Frederik Svane but held firm for a draw.With Gukesh's win already banked, Praggnanandhaa and Arjun Erigaisi didn't need to force matters either, settling for draws against Vincent Keymer and Matthias Bluebaum, respectively. India closed out the match 2.5-1.5.With the win, India moved to 15 points, still one point behind hosts Uzbekistan, who beat the United States on Friday to stay in front.India's women's team also had a productive Friday, with Vantika Agrawal and Divya Deshmukh both delivering important wins to seal the match against Uzbekistan.Vantika, playing white against Nilufarkhon Imomkuzieva, picked up an early pawn with a sharp tactical sequence; a check with her queen forced Black's king to give up material before the middlegame had properly begun.She nursed that small material edge through a long, technical battle, trading down into a rook endgame where her extra pawn and more active king proved decisive.Pushing her kingside pawns forward in the closing stages, Vantika eventually broke through, and Imomkuzieva had no way to hold the position together.Divya Deshmukh's game against Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova was a far longer and more chaotic affair.Both sides grabbed material early. Tokhirjonova's knight snatched a pawn on b7 just as Divya's queen picked up a stray piece on d2, leaving the position roughly balanced but sharp.What followed was a marathon battle through the middlegame and into a complex rook, knight and bishop endgame, with both players navigating tricky technical positions deep into the game.Divya's technique held up better over the long haul, and after 73 hard-fought moves, Tokhirjonova had nothing left to stop Black's advancing king, resigning the position.Those two results were enough to see India through the match, keeping the team firmly in the mix for a medal.As things stand, India's women sit second in the standings on 15 points, behind an in-form Chinese side on 17.With two rounds left, India's hopes of gold now depend largely on whether China slip up, but on Friday's evidence, neither Indian team looks inclined to make things easy for anyone chasing them either.In the Open section, India face Uzbekistan 2, while the women’s team take on China in the penultimate round of the Chess Olympiad.
Article Summary: Dommaraju gukesh beats germany's alexander donchenko in round 9 of the 46th chess olympiad in samarkand, uzbekistan. India's women's team also had a productive friday, with vantika agrawal and divya deshmukh both delivering important wins to seal the match. Tokhirjonova's knight snatched a pawn on b7 just as divya's queen picked up a stray piece on d2.

Article Title: At 17, British student Alex Chui scores a perfect 42/42 at the Maths Olympiad, winning his fifth gold medal in seven appearances
Article Text:
PC: UK Maths Trust

Alex Chui turns a perfect 42 into seven medals from seven IMO appearances

Britain returns from Shanghai with six medals

Six problems, 42 points and a 29-point gold medal cut-off in Shanghai

Seven medals across seven appearances

A perfect score is unusual at the International Mathematical Olympiad, where contestants face six demanding problems over two four-and-a-half-hour papers. According to UK Olympiads, in 2026, just seven of the 666 competitors managed to collect all 42 points. One of them was Britain’s Alex Chui, a 17-year-old from Tonbridge School.His result in Shanghai was also the latest entry in an unusual international record. Chui had already won gold medals at four previous editions of the competition. The 2026 gold made it five, while his appearances across seven editions produced seven medals in total. Britain finished ninth among 117 participating teams, with six medals shared between its six competitors.Chui’s 42 points came from six full-mark problems. He received 7 points on each question, leaving no partial score or missed mark on his final paper.The result placed him joint first individually. Only seven students reached the maximum score across the entire competition, which brought together 666 contestants representing 117 teams.Reportedly, for Chui, however, the perfect paper was part of a much longer record.He had already collected IMO gold medals in 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025. His fifth gold in Shanghai completed a run in which every one of his seven appearances produced a medal. That gives him seven medals from seven participations, including five golds.The British team finished with two golds, one silver and three bronze medals. Kevin Wai of Magdalen College School joined Chui in the gold-medal group after scoring 29 points. Yuvan Raja of RGS Guildford took silver with 26 points. Adavya Goyal of St Paul's School, along with Anango Prabhat and Michael Sydorenko of King's Maths School, each scored 22 and received bronze.The six students therefore all returned with medals. Their combined score was 163 points. That total placed Britain ninth in the team standings. North Korea also scored 163 points, but the two teams were separated by their medal distribution. North Korea had two golds and two silvers alongside two bronzes, while Britain had two golds, one silver and three bronzes.The International Mathematical Olympiad is built around six problems, divided between two examination days. Contestants have 4.5 hours on each day to tackle three questions. Each problem carries a maximum of seven points, giving a possible total of 42. The questions are designed around areas such as geometry, number theory, algebra and combinatorics, rather than the routine calculations associated with school mathematics.At the 2026 event in Shanghai, the results stretched from perfect scores at the top to a large number of contestants receiving no medal. There were 55 gold medals, 105 silvers and 189 bronzes, while 141 competitors received honourable mentions, as reported by The UK Olympiads and IMO2026.The gold threshold was 29 points. Wai's score landed exactly on that boundary.Chui's longer record is perhaps the most distinctive part of the 2026 result. His five IMO gold medals came in 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. The two remaining appearances also ended with medals, giving him seven medals from seven editions.The perfect 42 in Shanghai added another distinction to that record. Of the seven contestants who achieved a maximum score in 2026, Chui was the British representative, alongside three competitors from China, two from the United States and one from South Korea.At 17, his competition career at the IMO has now produced an unusually complete sequence: seven appearances, seven medals and five golds, capped by a 42-point performance in his latest contest.
Article Summary: Alex chui, 17, from tonbridge school, had already won gold at four previous editions of the international mathematical olympiad. The 2026 gold made it five, while his appearances across seven editions produced seven medals in total. Britain finished ninth among 117 participating teams, with six medals shared between its six competitors.

Article Title: Meet Zhang Zhanshuo: The 19-year-old who won seven golds at the Asian Games; from a kid who ‘couldn’t swim’ to a Chinese swimming star
Article Text:
His gold medals came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, along with three relay titles.

‘A seaside kid’ who had to learn to swim

Zhang started learning when he was around five and a half to six years old.

His family came from sport

The swimmer who keeps coming from behind

Seven golds and a new record

After touching the wall, Zhang sat on the lane line and counted his medals on his fingers. “1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7!”

He still gave himself '85 out of 100'

At six, Zhang Zhanshuo was the youngest swimmer in a local competition and had barely begun learning the sport. At 19, he left the Asian Games 2026 with seven gold medals and a place in the record books. The Chinese swimmer became the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single Asian Games when he won the men's 400m freestyle at the Aichi-Nagoya Games on September 25. His seven golds also equalled the Asian Games record for the most individual gold medals won at a single edition, a mark that had stood for 44 years. He competed in eight events and won seven of them. His gold medals came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, along with three relay titles. His 200m freestyle victory also produced an Asian record, while his 400m and 800m wins came in Games-record times. But Zhang's relationship with swimming began for a much simpler reason.Zhang was born in Qingdao in May 2007. His mother had been a middle-distance runner for the Shandong provincial team, while his father had also competed in athletics when he was younger, according to reports from Chinese media Qingdao.His father, Zhang Xunshan, has recalled that the original idea was not to turn his son into a professional swimmer. They lived in a coastal city, and he felt that a child growing up by the sea should at least know how to swim.Zhang started learning when he was around five and a half to six years old. As reported by Qingdao News, he trained for about half a year before entering the 2013 Qingdao primary and secondary school swimming competition. He was below the minimum age for the competition, but that did not stop him from taking part. The result surprised everyone. The six-year-old Zhang, the youngest competitor at the event, won six gold and two silver medals. At that stage, there was little indication that the boy would eventually become one of China's leading swimmers.A year later, Zhang was selected by Qingdao swimming coach Liu Ziqian and began systematic training with the city team. Liu later recalled that Zhang was the youngest swimmer in the group, training alongside athletes who were three or four years older.Zhang's parents understood the demands of competitive sport themselves. His mother had competed in middle-distance running for the Shandong provincial team, while his father had been involved in athletics. That background also helped his first coach recognise his physical potential. “When I took over, Zhang Zhanshuo was just over seven years old,” Liu told Qingdao Daily. “This child had talent from a young age because his mother had been a middle-distance runner for the Shandong team, and his father had also been an athlete when he was young. ”Zhang's rise was gradual after that. He began making a name for himself at provincial competitions before breaking through on the national stage as a teenager.By 16, he had won two gold medals at the 2023 Chinese National Swimming Championships. In 2024, he was part of China's world-championship-winning 4x200m freestyle relay team.One of Zhang's defining moments came during the men's 4x200m freestyle relay at the 2026 Asian Games. China was behind Japan going into the final leg. Zhang took over the anchor position and gradually closed the gap before overtaking Japan in the final stretch. His split was 1:42.92, and China finished in 7:00.17, breaking the Asian record. After the race, Zhang was asked about the dramatic comeback. His answer was short: “Normal, normal. ” His teammate Pan Zhanle had a very different way of describing what had just happened. Pan, who had previously been Zhang's childhood hero and was his teammate in the relay, called him a “miracle child” after the race.Zhang's biggest moment came four days later. On September 25, he won the men's 400m freestyle, setting a Games record and securing his seventh gold medal of the competition. After touching the wall, Zhang sat on the lane line and counted his medals on his fingers. “1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7!” “Just after I got out of the water, I counted my gold medals from one to seven. I wanted to express that I had won seven gold medals,” he told the media.His seven golds equalled the record for the most individual gold medals won at a single Asian Games. The previous record had belonged to North Korean shooter So Gil-san, who won seven golds at the 1982 New Delhi Games. Zhang also became the Chinese athlete with the most gold medals at a single Asian Games.Despite the seven gold medals, Zhang did not describe his Asian Games campaign as perfect. As reported by Xinhua, he gave himself a score of 85 out of 100 and said he still had technical areas to improve, particularly his turns. Zhang said after the Games: “One step short of perfect.” He also made it clear that the seven medals were not where he wanted the story to end. “The Asian Games is not the goal. I'm still aiming for the Olympics and competing with the best,” Zhang said, according to the South China Morning Post.
Article Summary: Zhang zhanshuo became the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single asian games. His gold medals came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, along with three relay titles. His mother had been a middle-distance runner for the shandong provincial team, while his father had also competed in athletics when he was younger.

Article Title: The next thing Adidas wants to make bespoke is the foam itself
Article Text:
An early prototype of Adidas's printed foam at the APEX Lab in Herzogenaurach

A foot model recreated from APEX scan data, used to build Project R.A.P. footwear

Running shoes have spent a decade getting faster through chemistry

Adidas's printed foam changes how it compresses through its structure, not a new formula

The Futurecraft 4D midsole, printed by Carbon as a lattice rather than moulded from foam. (Picture: Adidas)

Printed foam gets its behaviour from geometry

One of five printed foam versions Adidas made in three weeks.

Without a mould, foam can be remade for every athlete

Adidas's printed foam prototypes, which can be remade for each athlete without a mould.

Running-shoe foam has changed a great deal over the past decade, but it is still made in moulds, and a moulded midsole behaves the same way for every runner who wears that size. Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around that, though it has printed them from resin rather than foam.At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer. It was the final stop at the APEX Lab during Home of Innovation, the company's name for a tour through the labs where athletes test products most people won't see for another year or two. Chief Creative Officer Alasdhair Willis calls it "a future continuously being built." APEX, short for Athlete Product Excellence, is the elite-only room where Adidas makes bespoke products for its biggest names.Most of the tables there dealt with how a shoe gets customised to a single athlete. One covered the profile APEX builds before anything is made: 3D body and foot scans, pressure mapping and gait analysis, the process behind boots and shoes made for Lionel Messi, Anthony Edwards, Noah Lyles and Alexander Zverev.Another held Project R.A.P., short for Radical Athlete Perception, Adidas's 3D-printed footwear platform.Its lattice boots are made from an athlete's scan data and worn in MLS matches by Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan, and its basketball shoes by Brooklyn Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr.The last table came with a warning. Mateo, the designer behind it, said the project was at a very early stage, much further from production than R.A.P., and that the group was the first outside Adidas to see it. What he showed was printed foam, in structures that could be tuned in ways a moulded midsole cannot.Foam sits under almost every athletic shoe, but running is where the race to improve it has been fought most openly. For most of the last decade, progress in running-shoe cushioning has been a materials race. EVA, the light and cheap foam that sat under most shoes for years, gave way to expanded TPU, which Adidas brought to market as Boost in 2013. The next jump came from PEBA-based foams, which are lighter and return more energy, and which now sit under most elite racing shoes.Each step came from a lab working on the formula. A better foam meant a new polymer, a new blend or a new way of expanding it. Engineers could shape a midsole, stack layers or add a carbon plate, but the foam inside a moulded midsole behaves more or less the same throughout. Changing how it compresses has meant changing what it is made of.There is a practical reason for that. Foam midsoles are moulded, and a mould can only produce shapes that can be pulled back out of it. Complex internal structures are off the table, so the chemistry has had to carry most of the load.Adidas has found a way around that limit before. In 2017 it introduced Futurecraft 4D with Carbon, a printed midsole that gets its cushioning from a lattice structure, and 2021's 4DFWD added bowtie-shaped cells coded to compress forward under vertical impact. Those midsoles are printed as an elastomeric lattice, not foam in the EVA or Boost sense, so Adidas has been able to shape cushioning through geometry for some years, though never in foam.Mateo described printed foam as a combination of two things. From additive manufacturing it takes precision, control and customisation. From foam it keeps lightness, energy return and deformation, which he called a fancy word for how squishy it is. Adidas had to develop a new additive method to make it, though Mateo didn't say what the base material is.He was wearing one of the structures, so he walked up and down beside the table to show it working. This design is meant to maximise vertical deformation, meaning how far the foam compresses under load, and it does that by collapsing forward as the runner moves. You could see the cells fold in a set direction rather than squashing evenly, as a moulded slab would.The idea of a midsole that folds forward will be familiar from 4DFWD, which produced that movement with printed resin. The structure Mateo was wearing does it in foam, with the arrangement of its cells deciding how it compresses. He said this design was only one example, and a different structure could be optimised for weight, or built for walking rather than running, from the same material. A basketball shoe has to absorb heavy landings and support sharp cuts, while a walking shoe needs comfort over hours rather than speed over minutes. If the structure decides how the foam behaves, one printed material could in principle be shaped for each of those jobs.Geometry becomes more useful once it can be adjusted for an individual. Mateo said the lab can collect an athlete's pressure data, kinematics and foot scans, and then tune the structures to that athlete. That hasn't been possible with foam before, because a moulded midsole comes out the same for everyone in a size. APEX already profiles athletes across football, basketball, tennis and running, so the data needed to shape foam for one person is being collected well beyond runners.Speed matters as much as precision. Three weeks before the session, Mateo was at the factory where the samples on the table were made, and he produced five versions of the structure, each tuned differently. The process he described was simple: make a pair, test it with the athlete in the lab, adjust it, make another pair, and narrow down to the best shoe for that athlete.Alexander Taylor, Adidas's Senior Vice President of Innovation Design & Concepts, who was leading the group, put that pace in context. With conventional manufacturing, each change means working on moulds, and the structures on Mateo's table could not be moulded in the first place. Mateo has practically been living at the factory for the past three or four months, Taylor said, because the project now moves as quickly as he can test it. The shoes also look different, since the process produces shapes nothing from a mould would.For now, the project is being judged by how the structures behave rather than by numbers. Mateo didn't share energy-return figures to compare against moulded foams, and at this stage there may not be finished ones to share.Printed foam is still a long way behind R.A.P., which already has boots on an MLS pitch. If it follows the same path, its first wearers will be the athletes whose profiles are already on file at APEX, a few steps from the table where it was shown.
Article Summary: Adidas has been 3d-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around moulds. At its headquarters in herzogenaurach, adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer. It was the final stop at the apex lab during home of innovation. Adidas has developed a new additive method to make shoes.

Article Title: Minecraft Dungeons II to launch on September 29: Here's everything we know so far
Article Text:
Image credit: Mojang

Minecraft Dungeons II: Release date and platforms

Minecraft Dungeons II: A connected Minecraft world

New gear and character customisation

The Sift and the new story

Multiplayer changes in Minecraft Dungeons II

What makes the sequel different

Minecraft Dungeons II is set to launch tomorrow (September 29). Mojang is bringing its dungeon-crawling spin-off back with a new world, expanded gear systems and changes to exploration and multiplayer. The sequel follows the original Minecraft Dungeons, which launched in 2020 and attracted more than 25 million players before development ended. This time, the game moves away from its predecessor's mission-based structure and introduces a connected world players can explore on foot. It also adds jumping, new character customisation options, a new dimension called The Sift and more flexible multiplayer features.Mojang Studios and Double Eleven are developing the game, and it will be available on PC, current-generation consoles, and Nintendo’s latest systems. Here is everything players need to know about Minecraft Dungeons II before its September 29 release.Minecraft Dungeons II will launch on September 29, 2026, for PC through Steam and the Microsoft Store, Xbox Series X|S, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch and Nintendo Switch 2.There will be no PS4 or Xbox One version.The game will be available on Xbox Game Pass from day one. Xbox Play Anywhere support will also let players access compatible purchases across Xbox and PC.The Standard Edition costs $29.99, while the Deluxe Edition costs $49.99. The Deluxe Edition includes cosmetic items and the first two post-launch DLC packs.Players who pre-order before September 28 will also receive additional hero skins, a cape and a pet.One of the biggest changes is the move away from the mission-based structure of the original game. Minecraft Dungeons II introduces a connected world that players can travel through on foot instead of selecting individual missions from a central hub.Jumping has also been added for the first time. It lets players reach vertical areas, discover hidden locations, and approach combat differently. Weapons can also have unique jump attacks.The sequel retains the classless progression system but expands the ways players can customise their heroes. Armour is now divided into four pieces: head, chest, arms, and legs.Talismans provide passive bonuses, while artefacts return as active abilities. The enchantment system has also been changed, with new effects and rarities giving players more options when creating builds.Minecraft Dungeons II introduces The Sift, a new dimension created for the game. It has its own ecosystem, creatures and visual style, with inhabitants adapted to an environment that can also be dangerous for players.The story begins with the destruction of the camp from the first game, sending the heroes into a larger adventure. The Illager Council, made up of three powerful Illagers, serves as one of the threats. The game also features an environmental crisis, while side quests add detail about the world and its characters.The connected world changes as players progress, with characters needing help, areas developing, and shortcuts becoming available.Minecraft Dungeons II supports solo play and multiplayer, with built-in cross-platform support. Sessions can adjust when players join or leave, accommodating different group sizes.Players can also combine couch co-op with online multiplayer. This allows people playing together locally to join friends playing remotely. Matchmaking is available for players who want to join other groups.Minecraft Dungeons II expands the original formula without introducing character classes. Its main changes include a connected world, jumping, the Sift dimension, a larger gear system and more flexible multiplayer.Mojang Studios and Double Eleven, the teams behind the original game, are developing the sequel. It launches September 29 across current-generation consoles, PC and Nintendo’s current platforms, with Xbox Game Pass availability from day one.
Article Summary: Minecraft dungeons ii will launch on september 29, 2026, for pc through steam and the microsoft store. It will be available on current-generation consoles, pc and nintendo’s current platforms, with xbox game pass availability from day one. The standard edition costs $29.99, while the deluxe edition includes cosmetic items and the first two post-launch dlc packs.
